Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has resisted efforts by other Trump administration officials to restrict companies suspected of diverting Nvidia AI chips to China, sources tell Axios. Photo: Bonnie Cash/UPI/Bloomberg via Getty Images
President Trump on Thursday authorized a crack down on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China for the third time this year — even consulting Elon Musk before giving the go-ahead.
Why it matters: This standoff illustrates a breakdown in efforts to keep American technology out of China's hands as the world wonders why the Trump administration has not taken action against the company at the center of suspected chip smuggling — and an espionage scandal.
Inside the room: On Thursday, as the spy scandal rocked the administration, Lutnick met in the Situation Room with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and National Security Adviser and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Friction point: Lutnick's seemingly innocuous comment raised concerns, the sources said, because officials have repeatedly believed the Commerce Department would impose the export controls, only to have nothing happen.
This time, one person in the room called his bluff by saying: "Great. Why don't we do it today?"
Behind the scenes: With Lutnick the lone holdout, Trump made his decision: "Let's get it done." But once everyone was outside of the Oval Office, Lutnick proposed a new delay tactic.
The other side: Commerce Department spokesperson Kristen Eichamer denied that Bessent confronted Lutnick and would not immediately comment on the other allegations.
Flashback: On at least three separate occasions — in May, August, and Nov. 5 — Trump approved taking action against suspected diversions of Nvidia chips to China.
Catch up quick: The Trump administration last year announced it would loosen export controls on Nvidia H200 chip sales to China — something Nvidia has lobbied hard for.
The bottom line: While Lutnick oversees the department squarely at the center of export control policy, Trump is the ultimate decider.

Jensen Huang's potential ouster from Nvidia has plunged the AI industry into uncharted territory — a corporate earthquake that dwarfs even the chaos unleashed by Sam Altman's temporary firing from OpenAI in 2023.
Why it matters: Nvidia is the backbone of the global AI economy , with its chips, investments and financial guarantees sustaining an entire ecosystem of companies worth trillions of dollars.
Zoom in: As recently as two weeks ago, the notion of Nvidia without Jensen was unthinkable.
Driving the news: After that second affair came to light Wednesday night, Nvidia's board reportedly met to settle Huang's fate, though there was still no decision as of early Thursday morning. The White House was read in.
Zoom out: Huang's rise was the stuff of Silicon Valley legend: The Taiwanese immigrant went from cleaning toilets at a Kentucky boarding school and waiting tables at Denny's to building one of the most valuable companies in history.
The big picture: Huang's apparent downfall comes amid mounting anxiety over the AI industry's future, as new financial, political and regulatory risks threaten one of the largest infrastructure buildouts in history.
What to watch: The blast radius could extend far beyond Silicon Valley and Wall Street, threatening to engulf the Trump administration in a scandal over its handling of sensitive technology exports to China.
The bottom line: As veteran China watcher Bill Bishop wrote after Huang acknowledged his first affair: "There is rarely just one lie."

SEOUL — President Trump will get his wish for a historic meeting among the three most powerful men in the world — Xi Jinping of China, Vladimir Putin of Russia and himself — at a summit Thursday in southern China.
But Moscow, Beijing and Washington already know their leaders are arriving at the Shenzhen conference with disparate aims.
Trump hopes to focus the meeting on nuclear nonproliferation, urging the Russian and Chinese presidents to work with him to scale back the world’s largest nuclear stockpiles. Putin pressed for the meeting to discuss his ongoing war in Ukraine . And Xi wants to discuss neither, only embracing the idea of the summit to show the world China can help broker peace on the international stage, Chinese officials told The Times.
“That’ll be interesting,” Trump said earlier this week,  teasing the trilateral summit before the White House formally confirmed the meeting Friday.
“We’re talking a lot of things, including denuclearization,” he added, “but we’ll be talking a lot of things.”
U.S. officials have acknowledged they do not expect the meeting to result in a breakthrough on arms control. China is openly racing to build up its nuclear capacity — a nonnegotiable policy in Beijing, which sees its arsenal dwarfed by an American stockpile nearly 10 times the size.
“We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement. I would characterize this as the entry point,” one senior Trump administration official said. “This is the beginning of hopefully a conversation that can be productive going forward.”
Trump’s break from long-standing tradition in U.S.-Russia relations was real, but it should not have been entirely surprising.
The Chinese, too, threw cold water on the chances of a breakthrough, with one Chinese official telling The Times the central government saw no benefit to a pause.
“It is a matter of survival,” the official said.
The United States and Russia still command the world’s two dominant nuclear arsenals, with over 5,000 warheads each. China has an estimated 620 — but in catching up, it is developing new warheads with more sophisticated delivery systems.
Moscow, too, is modernizing its weapons, after the Trump administration allowed the last major U.S.-Russian nuclear arms treaty to expire earlier this year.
Though expectations are low for a nuclear breakthrough, Trump doesn’t want to discuss Putin’s priorities, either, the U.S. official added.
“He does not intend to talk about Ukraine in that meeting,” the official said. “China is not really part of that track, so it doesn’t really seem appropriate.”
Ukraine has grown increasingly concerned by Trump’s pressure campaign to force it into concessions to Moscow as he pushes to end the war.
The Trump administration has brought Russian and Ukrainian officials together at a working level to explore the viability of peace talks. But a long-standing U.S. policy on the war — not to negotiate about Ukraine without Ukraine — could be further compromised at a trilateral with Putin and Xi.
The only American business leader confirmed to join Trump in Asia is Elon Musk, the Tesla and SpaceX chief who was seen as instrumental in the decision last month to restrict Ukraine’s access on the battlefield to Starlink , the satellite internet service owned by Musk.
Beijing has struck a careful balance on Ukraine, publicly issuing its respect for sovereign borders — a position popular among Chinese voices who support Kyiv — while giving Moscow diplomatic cover, an economic lifeline and technological support throughout the war.
The summit’s stark lack of substance surprised even the closest China watchers.
Their competing agendas could make the summit little more than a spectacle, yet still produce images that hark back to the famous Yalta Conference — held in Crimea, the Ukrainian peninsula currently occupied by Russia, in 1945 — where Josef Stalin, Franklin Delano Roosevelt and Winston Churchill carved up a postwar order.
The summit on Chinese soil offers Xi a powerful image to broadcast worldwide , demonstrating an emergent superpower can bring together the leaders of two historic rivals in the name of peace.
Putin gets to present himself as a global player, despite the devastation wrought on Russia’s economy and military standing after four bruising years of war.
And it allows Trump to reassert his global relevance after this month’s midterms delivered the worst electoral rebuke to a president in half a century, rivaling the backlash against President Nixon during Watergate.

articles.title_orig: Cruise buffet controversy puts passengers who cut the line in the hot seat
articles.title_zh: Cruise buffet controversy puts passengers who cut the line in the hot seat
articles.content_orig:
A common cruise ship buffet habit is raising questions — and eyebrows — about what passengers should and shouldn’t do while filling their plates during meals.
Cutting ahead of others to grab just one item may seem a harmless action, but it can frustrate fellow passengers who have been patiently waiting their turn.
Buffet line-cutting was recently highlighted in a discussion about etiquette while at sea, according to the “ Royal Caribbean Blog .”
Passengers should wait their turn even if they only want something quick, such as a piece of toast or fruit, rather than squeezing past others or reaching around them, the blog advised.
Jumping ahead generally sends the wrong message, said Diane Gottsman, an etiquette expert based in Texas.
“It’s never acceptable to jump in front of someone in a buffet line, whether on a cruise ship , at a restaurant buffet or at a wedding,” Gottsman said.
“Everyone is waiting their turn, so having someone jump in front of you comes across as rude,” she added. “It also disrupts the flow of the buffet line, and in some cases can even cause a buffet traffic jam.”
There may be exceptions, however, depending on what someone needs and how crowded the buffet may be.
Gottsman said reaching in for a napkin is more understandable than cutting ahead to grab food. If only a few people are waiting, politely asking to step in briefly for a fork or knife may also be acceptable.
Holding a place for someone else can also test the patience of passengers who have been waiting.
“If you’re holding a space for your spouse, a friend or a child, the child generally gets a pass,” said Gottsman. But the spouse and friend are probably being judged and frustrating others who have been standing in line for 20 or 30 minutes.”
If another passenger does cut the line, however, Gottsman generally advises against confronting the person over a minor offense.
For someone who repeatedly jumps ahead, she suggested speaking with a manager in the dining area and allowing staff to handle the situation.
Cruise passengers themselves appear divided over exactly where to draw the line.
In a Reddit discussion, a traveler asked whether it was acceptable to skip ahead when people were waiting for the first dish at a buffet, but there was no line for other items farther down.
“If there’s a wide opening, it’s fine. If you’re squeezing in between people, then go wait in line like everyone else,” one person wrote.
Another commenter said the deciding factor should be whether the move holds up anyone already waiting.
“If they have to wait for you after getting [past] the first item, then you’ve cut in line,” the user wrote.
“No, get in the line,” another user chimed in.

articles.title_orig: Trump To Meet Xi, Putin In China For Nuclear Arms Talks; Ukraine Off Agenda
articles.title_zh: Trump To Meet Xi, Putin In China For Nuclear Arms Talks; Ukraine Off Agenda
articles.content_orig:
The meeting will be the first between the three leaders.
President Donald Trump will participate in the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the U.S., China and Russia on the sidelines at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in China next week, senior U.S. officials told reporters Friday evening.
Trump is expected to discuss Iran with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, the officials said, but he does not intend to discuss Russia's war with Ukraine during the trilateral meeting.
Denuclearization will be the focus of the long-awaited trilateral meeting, though officials do not anticipate the leaders reaching any concrete agreement and are characterizing this meeting as an initial conversation broaching the subject.
Trump had been teasing a potential face-to-face meeting with the world's leading nuclear superpowers for some time. On Oct. 19, Trump told ABC News that he would like to meet with Putin and Xi when he visits China, saying, "I would do that," and indicated a desire to discuss denuclearization.
Trump and Xi will meet ahead of their meeting with Putin but Trump and Putin will not be meeting one-on-one separately, the officials said.
Billionaire Elon Musk will be joining Trump for parts of his China travels, the officials said, but did not specify Musk's reason for accompanying the president, merely pointing to his business interests in China.
An official said some additional U.S. business leaders are expected to attend the APEC CEO Summit but clarified that they are not part of the U.S. delegation.
Trump's trip to Shenzhen, China, for the APEC Summit will be his second trip to China this year, as well and his third meeting with Xi . Before the China leg of the trip, Trump will be in Manila for the ASEAN Summit.
There are no plans for a meeting with North Korea's Kim Jung Un while Trump is in Asia, an official added.
The senior U.S. officials said they do not expect the Nvidia controversy of this week to have any impact on the president's trip or his planned meetings after former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned from the tech company over concerns that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Officials said they don't expect Trump to raise with Xi the allegations against Alice Huang, a Chinese national and tech executive at Megaspeed who is accused of being a Chinese spy, adding that the two presidents plan to focus on implementing aspects of their trade agreement.
"You know, I think when it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., it's probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," a senior U.S. official said.
Trump will depart from the White House on Monday morning en route to Manila, where he will participate in a series of multilateral meetings about peace and security in the Indo-Pacific region, the officials said. The president is also expected to sign a trade deal with Thailand, they added.
While in the Philippines, Trump will participate in a welcome ceremony and state visit with Philippines President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., followed by a bilateral meeting. Trump is expected to secure "commercial deals and strategic investments" during his two-day visit to the Philippines, officials said.
Trump will then travel to Shenzhen, where he will participate in an APEC leaders' dinner and multilateral meeting with the APEC leaders. On Thursday afternoon, Trump will participate in a bilateral meeting and working lunch with Xi.
The Trump-Xi-Putin meeting will be the final event on the president's Asia trip.

articles.title_orig: Italy fines Meta $887M for accessing Android users’ photos
articles.title_zh: Italy fines Meta $887M for accessing Android users’ photos
articles.content_orig:
Meta was fined €805 million in Italy yesterday over a Facebook for Android feature that suggests photos and videos from users' phone galleries for them to post.
The Garante, Italy's data protection authority, found that the feature was enabled by default and that the app accessed Italian users' photos, videos, and related metadata without their explicit consent.
The company has 60 days to switch the feature off by default, including for people who have already granted the app gallery access, and to request consent separately.
Meta plans to appeal and calls the fine "disproportionate", a spokesperson said in a statement reported by Reuters.
The app asks for gallery access via a single permission that covers the whole app and several functions with different purposes, the authority found. A general notice about enabling other features appears first, but it does not make it clear to users that they are also enabling gallery suggestions.
Fully granted, a permission like this lets the app read the phone's whole photo archive, usually on an ongoing basis. Neither the user nor the authority can check which information is actually used.
The authority found a breach of Article 122 of Italy's Privacy Code, which puts the EU's ePrivacy Directive into Italian law. That rule treats a phone as part of a person's private life. Any access to what the phone stores, therefore, requires free and informed consent, whether or not data is sent anywhere or harm results.
The authority's order, set out in its press release , requires the company to:
If the company misses the 60-day deadline, the feature cannot be switched on for anyone who has not given valid consent.
Meta said in a statement quoted in a Reuters report that the feature works only after users give permission on their device, and that they can change that permission at any time in their settings.
The Centro Tutela Consumatori Utenti, the Bolzano consumer protection group whose complaint started the investigation, published consumer advice on July 11, 2025. It told users to switch off the gallery suggestion settings in the app and to check what access and permissions the Facebook app has on their phone.
The investigation did not look at whether gallery content was used to train AI models. The company denies any such use. The authority may separately examine a newer feature, launched this year, that allows gallery content to be processed in the cloud.
The company had argued that Ireland's data protection authority should handle the case. The Garante rejected that argument because the ePrivacy rules do not provide a one-stop-shop mechanism.
The feature has been available since 2023. The investigation began in July 2025 and included the authority's own technical analysis.
The fine equals about 0.47% of the group's global revenue. In setting it, the authority weighed the large number of people involved, about 20 million Android users in Italy.
It also weighed how long the breach has lasted. The breach is still ongoing for people who have not updated the app, and for those who have already granted permission, the authority said.
Other factors were a 2019 decision against the company and limited cooperation during the investigation. Changes the company made after the complaint counted in its favor, though the authority judged them late and limited to people who update the app.

articles.title_orig: Russia's mega-rich are already imagining a post-Putin future
articles.title_zh: Russia's mega-rich are already imagining a post-Putin future
articles.content_orig:
Hours after launching his full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022, Vladimir Putin gathered Russia's richest men in the Kremlin's cavernous Yekaterininsky Hall.
More than three dozen of them sat huddled along a wall, wearing face masks because of the Covid pandemic. One Russian newspaper reporter described them as "pale and sleep-deprived". On entering, Putin sat down at the opposite side of the hall, creating a vast space between him and the businessmen. As usual, he was wearing no mask.
Using his typically coded language, he said he expected them to support the war.
"I would like to call on you to show understanding of what is going on," he said, "and work together with the government to find the tools which would support production, the economy, jobs."
In the Kremlin-published video of the meeting, none of the invited billionaires said a word.
That silence has become a feature of the Russian super-rich. Over the decades of Putin's rule, they have learnt that the price of piping up could be high. In 2003, oil magnate Mikhail Khodorkovsky, Russia's richest man at the time, who was funding a number of opposition groups, accused Putin of presiding over rampant corruption. He spent the next 10 years behind bars, convicted of tax evasion, fraud and embezzlement - a warning to other would-be critics. He denied the charges.
And even if any of the tycoons objected to the war, they have tended to keep their thoughts to themselves.
But even in that silence, there are murmurings: some members of Russia's once-mighty business elite seem to be imagining a Russia after Putin. They are wondering if, once the president has left office or died, the country might look more like it did in the 1990s, when the oligarchs enjoyed the fruits of power - or even if a healthier politics may take root.
The journalist Arkady Ostrovsky, a prominent Kremlin-watcher at The Economist newspaper who recently spent hours interviewing one of Russia's richest men, says he feels that a "historic, political shift is happening" in terms of how the ultra-rich view the future of the country.
The collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 gave birth to a new, powerful force on the domestic scene: people who took advantage of the end of communism and became extraordinarily rich, and then wanted to control politicians for their own benefit. They were dubbed "the oligarchs", from Ancient Greek for the "few who rule".  They had money, which back then meant power.
This era of the "wild 1990s" was when the so-called "new Russians" burst onto the scene. Huge state companies came up for grabs, and men with the right connections became millionaires - even billionaires - almost overnight. Corruption was rife, cronyism rampant, and contract killings frequent.
But almost immediately after Putin was first elected as president in 2000, he subjugated the oligarchs. He had little interest in sharing power with anyone else. He could afford to stand up to the billionaires because Russia's economy was getting back on its feet, and the central government was getting stronger.
Bill Browder, a financier who used to be the biggest foreign investor in Russia, and was banned from the country in 2005 after campaigning against corruption, says the Russian tycoons cowered and wilted in front of Putin - for example at the Davos economic forum, in the pre-war years when they were still welcomed there.
"I can remember seeing oligarchs walking around like they own the place, the most arrogant and self-confident individuals. And then Putin showed up, and it was just remarkable to see how these supposedly alpha-male-on-steroids individuals turned into absolutely subordinate, almost desperate schoolchildren," he tells the BBC.
Since the outbreak of war in 2022, the Kremlin has kept Russia's rich businessmen in line with a ruthless policy of carrot and stick. Critics of the war have seen their assets seized, while loyalists have been rewarded with lavish government war contracts: today there are more Russian billionaires than ever (155 in total, according to Forbes magazine).  Their collective wealth has reached a new high of nearly $700bn (£525bn).
But even for those tycoons who have stayed loyal and been rewarded, all of that money doesn't seem to be making them happy. Some are growing restless.
Their billions do not go as far as they used to: domestically, they cannot buy much political influence.
"They have no cards, they have no game," exiled politician and analyst Dmitry Nekrasov says. "They're rich because they've got something to do with Putin, not the other way round."
And outside of Russia, they are ostracised because of the Western sanctions imposed on Russia after its full-scale invasion.
"They're treated like low-level criminals. They can't fly their private jets. Their yachts can't park in all the best harbours in Europe. It must be very awful and humiliating for them," says Browder, the avowed Putin critic.
And so, quietly, some of their minds are turning to what happens after Putin leaves the scene. That's what I'm told by well-placed analysts, who are immersed in the world of these tycoons.
There's no immediate prospect of the president's departure, and there's no reason to think he's in bad health. But Putin, who turned 74 last month, has served in the Kremlin for a quarter of a century; people in Moscow know that his exit will come one day. When asked by Reuters last year if he intends to serve until 2036, when his constitutional term technically ends, Putin replied: "Only God knows if we have enough health."
If Putin resigned or died in office, the prime minister, Mikhail Mishustin, would take over. But Mishustin has not exhibited any presidential ambitions (that's probably a key reason he was appointed). That would create something of a power vacuum.
In that scenario, Russia-watchers I have spoken with envisage a few potential scenarios.
Some in the West, and no doubt within Russia, hope that democracy might flourish in a post-Putin Russia, with government led by the people, rather than by a new cadre of oligarchs or a single autocrat. But this seems like the least likely path, analysts say. Key democratic institutions have been eroded or destroyed over Putin's rule. "Russia is so used to violence, it has grown unaccustomed to standard democratic procedures," says Alexandra Prokopenko, an exiled Russian journalist and analyst.
Another path is more autocracy. A different figure could replace Putin and continue his culture of repression. But Prokopenko thinks this wouldn't be another strongman dictatorship - at least not right away. These things take time, she says: at first, Putin's successor would be weaker than him, with fewer resources.
And then there's the third option: tycoons re-assert their power and Russia returns to something resembling a 1990s-style system of oligarchy. Dmitry Nekrasov, a former Kremlin adviser and opposition politician who now lives in exile, says under this scenario, the country would be governed by a handful of powerful elite clans in alliance with business interests.
This last option, of course, is the one that many tycoons want. "They'd like to return to a time when they were listened to, when they were not stripped of assets and when they understood the rules of the game," says Prokopenko, who has spent a lot of time speaking to Russia's richest people.
Though their power has been seriously curtailed since the 1990s, it's still worth listening to the tycoons: given their immense wealth, it seems likely that sooner or later they will try to re-assert their political influence.
Already, some are "trying to be friends with the right sort of security officials or ministers", says Nekrasov, the exiled politician. But he says any further steps are "too dangerous to take".

articles.title_orig: Eisenkot says Netanyahu can’t remain Israel PM amid alleged vote meddling
articles.title_zh: Eisenkot says Netanyahu can’t remain Israel PM amid alleged vote meddling
articles.content_orig:
Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has said Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu cannot “remain at the helm of government for even one more minute” amid reports alleging Netanyahu’s office engaged in electoral interference.
Eisenkot, tasked with forming Israel’s new government , launched a scathing attack on his rival on Sunday, just a few hours after representatives of the two men met to discuss the possible formation of a national unity government .
“The conduct of outgoing Prime Minister Netanyahu and his inner circle poses a tangible, direct and immediate threat to Israeli democracy,” Eisenkot wrote on X.
Israeli broadcaster Channel 12 published a report earlier on Sunday alleging Netanyahu’s chief of staff, Ido Norden, lodged a complaint with the police commissioner’s office against members of the United Arab List (Ra’am) party on the eve of Israel’s October 27 election .
Norden reportedly directed police officers to an alleged intelligence source who was a former employee of Netanyahu’s office.
Based on information from the source, about 14 police officers raided the homes of three Ra’am members without a warrant and arrested them on suspicion of bribery to incentivise voting, according to Channel 12.
Netanyahu subsequently launched a campaign against Arab-led parties throughout election day. After they won a record 19 seats, he made unproven accusations of electoral fraud.
The three men were released after police determined the information from the purported intelligence source was unfounded.
The Channel 12 report also alleged that David Zini, the head of Israel’s internal intelligence agency Shin Bet, requested the attorney general’s office to wiretap five Palestinian-Israeli Knesset members on election day over suspected election interference, but the request was later rejected.
“I call for an immediate investigation into the affair and for the police and the Shin Bet to immediately clarify the details that have been published,” said Eisenkot, a former army chief.
Netanyahu’s Likud party called Eisenkot’s statement “outrageous incitement” against the prime minister.
On Friday, Eisenkot accused Netanyahu of fuelling a “racist and violent” campaign against Palestinian citizens of Israel during the elections to cling to power.
Netanyahu renewed his appeal to Eisenkot to form a unity government on Saturday, but the opposition leader called the plea a “bluff”.
However, Eisenkot had confirmed talks between his Yashar party and the Likud party over the proposal for a shared government.
Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot’s bloc has yet secured the 61 seats needed to form a government.

articles.title_orig: Thousands of US flights cancelled or delayed two days after grounding of planes nationwide
articles.title_zh: Thousands of US flights cancelled or delayed two days after grounding of planes nationwide
articles.content_orig:
Thousands of US flights were cancelled or delayed on Sunday as the US air-traffic control system continued to recover from a technical failure that led to a rare national ground stop.
Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said normal operations may not be restored until Monday.
"We have airplanes and crews that are out of position, so it takes a little bit of time," he told the BBC's US partner CBS. More than 8,800 flights were delayed and 2,400 cancelled on Sunday.
President Donald Trump urged Congress on Sunday to approve more money to modernise the air-traffic control system. The grounding of all aircraft scheduled to depart the US on Friday caused chaos at airports across the country.
More than 3,500 airplanes were in the air when the FAA announced at 15:54 EST (20:54 GMT) that flights would be grounded until further notice. Some were diverted to other airports and others flew on to their destinations.
In the aftermath, 8,500 flights were delayed and another 8,000 cancelled, according to FlightAware.
The stoppage left passengers stuck inside planes on the tarmac, unable to take off or to return to their gates. Others were stranded in airports, sleeping on the floor and desperately trying to get in touch with their airline. The ground stop also had a knock-on effect on schedules around the world, with some flights out of the UK and Europe cancelled.
The ground stop was lifted after about four and a half hours, but the impacts continued over the weekend.
On Saturday, airlines cancelled more than 5,900 flights and more than 7,000 others were delayed.
Investigators are still working to determine the root cause and who is at fault, but Duffy said the administration decided to ground flights after failures in a key system that allows air traffic controllers and pilots to communicate.
The transport secretary said a computer router installed as part of an upgrade from copper wire to fibre started sending out faulty signals.
He said on Sunday that the router - a piece of equipment which directs traffic across the network - was installed in El Dorado, Arkansas, and "flooded our network".
Duffy said that issues will continue to arise until the US makes major modernising changes to its air control system. The system needs a complete overhaul, he said.
"Let's not lie to each other," he said on NBC's Meet The Press. "We have to make investments into a network that has been neglected for decades."
In a post on Truth Social on Sunday, Trump urged US lawmakers to allocate the money, saying "we can get it built quickly and efficiently".
"It will be the BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the World. Much of our current air control system is 50 years old - RIDICULOUS! We have already started the work, but it should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs," he said.
Experts say the US uses antiquated technology for flight communications.
Aviation analyst Miles O'Brien described the US system as "a house that's about to be condemned".
He told the BBC: "I think most of us could look at this and go 'this is a system in the United States that we have allowed to decay'. It is worse than a fixer-upper."

articles.title_orig: Megaspeed Says Alice Huang Left Company in August 2025
articles.title_zh: Megaspeed Says Alice Huang Left Company in August 2025
articles.content_orig:
Megaspeed, the Singaporean data center company, said in a statement on Sunday that Alice Huang, a former executive at the center of what U.S. officials call a Chinese spy plot targeting the Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, had left the company in August 2025.
The statement, which was reported by The Associated Press, was Megaspeed’s first to directly address the status of Ms. Huang since she became the focus of international scrutiny over her ties to Mr. Huang, who resigned from Nvidia on Thursday.
News of their relationship rocked Nvidia, the dominant maker of artificial intelligence chips, as well as the global technology sector and the U.S. government.
Last month, The New York Times reported that American officials had concluded Ms. Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset and had a close relationship with Mr. Huang, one of the most powerful figures in the A.I. boom and an adviser to President Trump.
Mr. Huang acknowledged last Sunday that he’d had an affair with Ms. Huang, and Nvidia’s board of directors said they had begun an investigation into his conduct . On Wednesday, The New York Times reported that he also had an extramarital relationship with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him. He abruptly stepped down as chief executive the next day from the company he had led for more than 30 years.
The chip maker’s stock has fallen about 30 percent below its all-time high, which was set just over a month ago, erasing more than $1 trillion in market value.

articles.title_zh: Third US aircraft carrier enters Middle East as Trump heads to China for talks with Xi, Putin
articles.content_orig:
The meeting will be the first between the three leaders.
President Donald Trump will participate in the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the U.S., China and Russia on the sidelines at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in China next week, senior U.S. officials told reporters Friday evening.
Trump is expected to discuss Iran with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, the officials said, but he does not intend to discuss Russia's war with Ukraine during the trilateral meeting.
Denuclearization will be the focus of the long-awaited trilateral meeting, though officials do not anticipate the leaders reaching any concrete agreement and are characterizing this meeting as an initial conversation broaching the subject.
Trump had been teasing a potential face-to-face meeting with the world's leading nuclear superpowers for some time. On Oct. 19, Trump told ABC News that he would like to meet with Putin and Xi when he visits China, saying, "I would do that," and indicated a desire to discuss denuclearization.
Trump and Xi will meet ahead of their meeting with Putin but Trump and Putin will not be meeting one-on-one separately, the officials said.
Billionaire Elon Musk will be joining Trump for parts of his China travels, the officials said, but did not specify Musk's reason for accompanying the president, merely pointing to his business interests in China.
An official said some additional U.S. business leaders are expected to attend the APEC CEO Summit but clarified that they are not part of the U.S. delegation.
Trump's trip to Shenzhen, China, for the APEC Summit will be his second trip to China this year, as well and his third meeting with Xi . Before the China leg of the trip, Trump will be in Manila for the ASEAN Summit.
There are no plans for a meeting with North Korea's Kim Jung Un while Trump is in Asia, an official added.
The senior U.S. officials said they do not expect the Nvidia controversy of this week to have any impact on the president's trip or his planned meetings after former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned from the tech company over concerns that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Officials said they don't expect Trump to raise with Xi the allegations against Alice Huang, a Chinese national and tech executive at Megaspeed who is accused of being a Chinese spy, adding that the two presidents plan to focus on implementing aspects of their trade agreement.
"You know, I think when it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., it's probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," a senior U.S. official said.
Trump will depart from the White House on Monday morning en route to Manila, where he will participate in a series of multilateral meetings about peace and security in the Indo-Pacific region, the officials said. The president is also expected to sign a trade deal with Thailand, they added.
While in the Philippines, Trump will participate in a welcome ceremony and state visit with Philippines President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., followed by a bilateral meeting. Trump is expected to secure "commercial deals and strategic investments" during his two-day visit to the Philippines, officials said.
Trump will then travel to Shenzhen, where he will participate in an APEC leaders' dinner and multilateral meeting with the APEC leaders. On Thursday afternoon, Trump will participate in a bilateral meeting and working lunch with Xi.
The Trump-Xi-Putin meeting will be the final event on the president's Asia trip.

With Bitcoin ( BTC +2.52% ) currently trading under $70,000, now might not seem like the best time to be loading up on the world's most popular cryptocurrency. After all, Bitcoin is still 45% below its all-time high of $126,000 from last October.
But there are plenty of analysts and investors who think this could be a fantastic time to buy Bitcoin . Among them is Galaxy Digital ( GLXY -5.27% ) , which recently published a report called "Why Now Is the Time to Add and Hold Bitcoin" that makes a strong buy case for Bitcoin.
According to Galaxy Digital, based on a reading of the historical data, Bitcoin hit a bottom at $60,000 this summer, and is now in the accumulation phase.
As Galaxy Digital points out, Bitcoin is highly cyclical , typically following a four-year pattern of boom and bust. If Bitcoin continues the same pattern that has repeated after the 2014, 2018, and 2022 crypto downturns, then Bitcoin could be ready to go on another of its parabolic runs.
Image source: Getty Images.
Moreover, Galaxy suggests that the sellers are mostly gone as the short-term momentum traders and speculators who rushed into crypto when Bitcoin was soaring past $100,000 have now been washed out. The only money that's left is the long-term money with buy-and-hold conviction . That's going to help to put a floor under the price of Bitcoin.
CRYPTO · As of 9:05 PM ET 11/15/26
Finally, the macroeconomic situation in the U.S. -- mounting deficits, rising inflation, and a $40 trillion national debt load -- all point to currency debasement . In other words, the thinking is that the U.S. government will need to print money to get out of a financial jam, and that's going to end up reducing the value of the U.S. dollar. As a result, many investors may turn to Bitcoin as a potential hedge against inflation and currency debasement.
The question on many Bitcoin investors' minds is, of course: How much higher Bitcoin can go over the next few years? If history is any guide, the upside potential might range from 7.6x to 87x. That's how much Bitcoin rose in previous market cycles, according to Galaxy Digital.
Of course, history does not always repeat, so relying just on past trends to invest would be unwise. However, I'm optimistic. While there's plenty of reason for concern, Bitcoin appears to be a coiled spring right now. I'm fully expecting it to shrug off the current market malaise and march higher over the next 12 months. If Bitcoin doesn't hit $100,000 next year, I'll be very surprised.

articles.title_orig: US FDA declines to approve Summit lung cancer drug after trial misses key survival goal
articles.title_zh: US FDA declines to approve Summit lung cancer drug after trial misses key survival goal
articles.content_orig:
The Food and Drug Administration rejected a first-of-its-kind cancer drug that was invented in China, a setback for a medicine that had become a symbol of China’s ascendance as a powerhouse in drug development.
Summit Therapeutics, the Florida company that has been seeking to bring the drug to the American market, disclosed the agency’s decision in a news release on Sunday . Summit bought the U.S. rights to the drug from Akeso Biopharma, a Chinese drugmaker that invented the drug in its laboratories and sells it in China.
Summit had been seeking approval only for certain patients with advanced lung cancer. But the drug had raised high hopes because it is being tested in many more cancers, including tumors of the colon, bladder and breast.
Summit said on Sunday that the F.D.A. told the company it had rejected the drug because it had not shown a statistically significant benefit in prolonging patients’ lives in the global clinical trial that was the basis of Summit’s application.
Summit had been seeking F.D.A. approval based on the results of a study the company conducted in the United States, Canada, Europe and Asia that enrolled patients who had already tried a targeted treatment. The trial compared patients who received ivonescimab and chemotherapy with those whose only treatment was chemotherapy. In that study, the drug was successful in delaying the cancer’s progression.
Summit has argued that the failure to extend patients’ lives simply reflected slow enrollment in the study. Hoping to bolster its case, the company had sent the F.D.A. analyses that were not specified in the original research plan of patients’ longer-time outcomes, but those were not enough to persuade regulators.

articles.title_orig: Vulcan rocket fails during launch, dealing major blow to SpaceX competitors
articles.title_zh: Vulcan rocket fails during launch, dealing major blow to SpaceX competitors
articles.content_orig:
United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket and 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites fell back to Earth minutes after liftoff Sunday, a crushing setback that will ripple across all sectors of the US space industry.
The Vulcan rocket is on contract to launch roughly half of the US military’s national security space missions in the next few years, and Sunday’s mission was the first of 38 Vulcan launches booked by Amazon to build out its network of broadband Internet satellites aimed at competing with SpaceX’s Starlink. Sunday’s failure is expected to ground the rocket for an indefinite period of time.
Vulcan is no stranger to close calls, having overcome failures with its strap-on solid rocket boosters on two of its four previous flights. In each case, the rocket corrected for those problems and continued into orbit to deploy its payloads. The incidents trigged months-long reviews and investigations before ULA could resume Vulcan flights.
Sunday’s launch succumbed to a different kind of failure. The six solid rocket boosters appeared to perform well in the first two minutes after Vulcan’s liftoff from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, at 12:40 pm EDT (17:40 UTC).
In a statement, ULA said the rocket “suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit.” The company said it did not immediately have “any specific data to understand what occurred.”
“ULA exists to provide assured access to space for our nation and for the customers who depend on us,” the company said in a statement. “That purpose is why we take on some of the hardest missions in spaceflight, and why we hold ourselves to the standard of mission success. Today, we did not meet that standard.”
Engineers will investigate the failure to “find the cause, determine the appropriate corrective action, and return to flight as quickly as possible,” ULA said.
“ULA is committed to full transparency with our customers, and they will have visibility into the investigation process, which utilizes rigorous methodology and corrective action. We will provide further updates when new information becomes available.”
The first indications of trouble Sunday appeared to crop up before the 10-minute mark of the flight, the point in time when ULA initially said the anomaly occurred.
Multiple sources told Ars the anomaly that impacted the launch occurred in the booster stage of the rocket, not the Centaur V upper stage or the solid rocket boosters. It could not immediately be determined whether the booster stage issue was caused by the two methane-burning BE-4 engines that power it, some other part of the booster that feeds propellant into the engines, or another problem.
Heading northeast from Cape Canaveral, Vulcan jettisoned its spent solid rocket boosters on time, leaving the launcher flying on the power of its twin BE-4 main engines supplied by Blue Origin, Jeff Bezos’s space company. The BE-4s, each designed to produce more than a half-million pounds of thrust, were supposed to shut down just shy of the flight’s five-minute mark. However, they continued firing for at least 30 additional seconds.
Such an overburn could be an indication the booster stage was not performing as expected and operated longer to try to compensate for the underperformance.
A mission animation on ULA’s broadcast, driven by real-time telemetry data from the rocket, showed Vulcan start to spin moments after booster engine shutdown. The spin continued through separation of the rocket’s Centaur V upper stage a few seconds later. ULA’s launch commentator confirmed ignition of the Centaur’s two RL10 engines, and the animation showed them vectoring thrust in an apparent attempt to put the rocket back on course.
ULA ended its live broadcast a few minutes later without discussion of the anomaly. The company then released a statement on social media declaring the launch a failure. This was the first total mission failure for United Launch Alliance since its formation in 2006 with the merger of the rocket divisions of Boeing and Lockheed Martin.
Sunday’s incident is bad news for ULA’s two primary customers: Amazon and the US Space Force. It’s also a potential setback for NASA’s Artemis program to return astronauts to the Moon.
First, Amazon. The loss of 40 Amazon Leo satellites onboard the Vulcan rocket is, by itself, a secondary concern next to the inevitable grounding of the company’s primary launch provider. Amazon has 37 more Vulcan launches reserved with ULA, each of which is slated to deliver 40 or more Amazon Leo satellites to orbit.
The Amazon Leo constellation today consists of 396 satellites, a fraction of the network’s planned total of 3,292 first-generation spacecraft. Amazon officials told Ars in October that the company has enough satellites to start initial commercial Internet service by the end of the year, but more launches are required to realize the network’s full capacity.
Amazon is setting up its service as the first head-to-head competitor in the consumer satellite broadband market with the Starlink network owned by Elon Musk and SpaceX. OneWeb and other companies also offer Internet connectivity from space, but their business models focus on beaming capacity to traditional telco providers, not directly to consumers.
Previous delays with the Vulcan rocket have kept Amazon satellites on the ground far longer than the company planned. Amazon recently announced it manufactured its 1,000th satellite, meaning more than half of its network nodes are sitting in storage. Finally, Amazon was looking forward to ramping up its launch cadence, with Sunday’s launch the first for Amazon Leo on ULA’s Vulcan rocket.
“There is risk with any launch, and that’s especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01,” Amazon said in a statement. “ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they’ll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan.”
Amazon made launch bookings with Europe’s Arianespace and Bezos’s Blue Origin at the same time it signed the contract for 38 Vulcan launches in 2022. Amazon reserved additional launches with Arianespace in September, bringing that company’s total contract to 24 launches for Amazon. Three have launched so far, and the fourth is set to take off later this month on an Ariane 6 rocket from French Guiana.
Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket has also encountered setbacks on its early missions. Most recently, a New Glenn rocket exploded during a ground test in Florida in May, knocking Blue Origin’s launch pad offline until at least the end of this year. The New Glenn that exploded was supposed to launch a batch of Amazon Leo satellites, but luckily for Amazon, the payloads were not stacked aboard the rocket at the time.
What’s more, the New Glenn rocket uses a version of the BE-4 engine similar to the one that flies on ULA’s Vulcan rocket. Investigators traced the New Glenn explosion to a faulty valve on one of the booster’s BE-4 engines. If engineers determine a BE-4 was at fault on Sunday’s Vulcan failure, it could stand in the way of Blue Origin returning New Glenn to flight early next year.
That would mean more delays for two of the rockets Amazon needs to get its satellites in orbit. Amazon’s past rocket woes forced officials to contract with SpaceX, Bezos’s chief competitor in the satellite broadband and launch sectors, to use its workhorse Falcon 9 rocket to speed up Amazon Leo deployment. Amazon has 10 more missions booked on SpaceX’s Falcon 9, and will presumably be unable to buy more as SpaceX moves the rocket toward retirement.
It’s a similar story for the Space Force, which relies upon SpaceX and ULA to launch the military’s most sensitive national security satellites. The Space Force in 2025 added Blue Origin’s New Glenn as a third option to launch the country’s critical military payloads.

articles.title_zh: Nvidia Fallout Looms Over Trump-Xi Meeting
articles.content_orig:
At major moments in President Trump’s second term, he has looked up during an economic speech or diplomatic dinner and asked a version of the same question: “Where’s Jensen?”
Jensen Huang has usually been out there, somewhere in the room.
Mr. Huang, who was until Thursday the leather-jacketed chief executive of Nvidia, one of the world’s largest companies, had impressed the president with his success, his money and his argument that keeping China dependent on American-made semiconductor chips and technology could help maintain U.S. dominance over Beijing.
Mr. Trump made sure to have the technology executive with him during pivotal U.S.-China meetings this year. The president invited him to come to China in May when he went to meet with Xi Jinping, China’s leader, stopping in Alaska , where Mr. Huang joined him on Air Force One at the last minute. And Mr. Huang was at the head table with the president when Mr. Trump hosted a state dinner for Mr. Xi at the White House in September.
But when Mr. Trump travels to China for another meeting with Mr. Xi at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation in Shenzhen this week, Mr. Huang, the man who has been influential in shaping the president’s views about technological competition with China, is not expected to be at his side.
Last week, Mr. Huang stepped down from his role at Nvidia after revelations that he had engaged in affairs, including one with Alice Huang , a woman who U.S. intelligence officials believe is an asset of Beijing.
Mr. Huang’s sudden fall and the U.S. finding that he was targeted by Chinese intelligence do not appear to have altered Mr. Trump’s estimation of the former Nvidia leader — or his approach to dealing with his Chinese counterpart in this week’s meeting. (Beijing has called the U.S. intelligence conclusions “smears and slanders.”)

articles.title_orig: Police ban protests near 10 schools and five universities in Paris
articles.title_zh: Police ban protests near 10 schools and five universities in Paris
articles.content_orig:
Police in Paris have issued a five-day ban on protests near 10 secondary schools and five universities as authorities try to control weeks of blockades and violence at educational venues in France.
The order prohibits unauthorised gatherings or marches within 100m of the sites from 16 to 20 November.
Paris police chief Patrice Faure said the ban was necessary due to "numerous disruptions and blockades around certain secondary schools and establishments of higher learning" and "persistent violence".
A wave of protests began in France September over poor secondary school conditions, before spreading to universities, workers and a "yellow-vest" movement against the cost of living.
Announcing the order, the Paris police chief said blockades around certain secondary schools and universities have led to damaged public property, violence against members of the educational community and clashes with law enforcement.
Mayors of eight Parisian districts had contacted the regional education authority to call for measures to "secure the entrances and exits" of blockaded secondary schools, local media report.
Some 1,548 people have been arrested in Paris since the start of the protests, Faure said on Sunday.
On Saturday, 106,000 people from a range of groups took to the streets in France, including 24,000 in Paris, the interior ministry said.
It marked the fifth Saturday in a row where students, unions and yellow-vest activists went out to protest.
The number of protesters was much lower than previously, and so was the number of those arrested, the ministry said - 219 across the country, including 45 in Paris.

articles.title_orig: Popular pasta chain closing over 40 more restaurants
articles.title_zh: Popular pasta chain closing over 40 more restaurants
articles.content_orig:
Noodles & Company NDLS reported higher comparable sales and a narrower loss in the third quarter of 2026, as increased customer traffic and sales transferred from closed restaurants helped improve margins.
Revenue fell $1.2 million from a year earlier to $120.9 million as restaurant closures offset sales growth at locations that remained open. The company reported a net loss of $2.1 million, or $0.36 per diluted share, compared with a loss of $9.2 million, or $1.58 per diluted share, a year earlier.
Systemwide comparable restaurant sales rose 9.5%, including a 10.7% increase at company-owned restaurants and a 4.9% gain at franchised locations. Company-owned comparable traffic grew 7.8%, while average check increased 2.6%, including 1.9% effective pricing.
CEO Joe Christina said the results marked the company’s eighth consecutive quarter of positive same-store sales growth. Average unit volume at company restaurants rose 15.2% to $1.54 million.
Restaurant contribution margin improved to 16.7% from 13.2% a year earlier, while adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, or adjusted EBITDA, rose 34% to $8.7 million.
Chief Financial Officer Mike Hynes said sales leverage helped reduce labor costs as a percentage of sales, while menu pricing, favorable mix and lower food waste contributed to a decline in cost of sales as a percentage of revenue. The quarter’s loss included a $1.2 million noncash impairment charge, primarily related to decisions to close certain restaurants.
Noodles closed 12 company-owned restaurants during the quarter. It also opened one franchise restaurant and closed two franchised locations. Hynes estimated that sales transferred from recently closed restaurants to nearby locations benefited third-quarter company comparable sales by approximately 3 percentage points.
In response to a question from StoneX analyst Todd Brooks, Hynes said the company had pulled forward some closures, reducing expected revenue without hurting profitability. Brooks noted that the company had lowered the upper end of its previous revenue guidance by about $5 million.
Hynes said the portfolio optimization process was winding down and that management’s current estimate was for 10 to 15 closures in 2027, although there was no firm number. Some would result from natural lease expirations rather than early closures under the optimization program, he said.
Ramen launch and October sales
Comparable sales rose 5.5% in October, following 8% growth in the same month of 2025, when the company launched its Chili Garlic Ramen limited-time offering. Noodles introduced ramen as a permanent menu category in October 2026, and Christina said the new lineup accounted for a double-digit percentage of product mix during the month.
Christina said the company trained restaurant teams in September and emphasized marketing during the first weeks of the launch to build awareness and encourage trial. Noodles plans to rotate additional ramen dishes into the menu during 2027.
Hynes said the current ramen offerings were not hurting average check. Two of the dishes come with protein, while a third without a set protein offers a lower entry point, he said.
Christina also highlighted the August launch of Baked Cheese Tortelloni. Among new guests who tried it, the dish had the highest return rate of products launched this year, he said. For 2027, the company is testing products across its Asian, Italian and macaroni-and-cheese categories, as well as ramen.
Full-year outlook and debt
Noodles tightened its full-year 2026 guidance, projecting revenue of $485 million to $495 million and comparable restaurant sales growth of 9% to 10%. It expects restaurant contribution margin of 16% to 16.7% and adjusted EBITDA of $35 million to $37 million.
The company forecast 34 to 36 company-owned restaurant closures and seven to eight franchise closures for the year, along with one new franchise opening. It expects capital expenditures of $8.5 million to $9.5 million and remains on track to generate positive free cash flow, according to Hynes.
At the end of the third quarter, Noodles had $1.5 million in available cash and $101 million in debt, down $9.2 million from the end of 2025. Hynes said the company sees an opportunity to reduce debt to approximately $100 million by year-end.
The company also announced an amendment extending its credit facility’s maturity date to Nov. 30, 2027. Hynes said the extension and improved business results provide additional flexibility as Noodles continues its review of strategic alternatives.
About Noodles & Company NDLS
Noodles & Company is a fast-casual restaurant company headquartered in Broomfield, Colorado. Founded in 1995, the company operates restaurants serving dishes inspired by noodle and pasta traditions from around the world, with a menu designed to offer customizable meals in a casual setting. Its menu includes noodle-based entrées such as Wisconsin Mac & Cheese, Japanese Pan Noodles, Pad Thai and spaghetti, along with salads, soups, desserts and beverages. The company also offers options intended to accommodate various dietary preferences, including vegetarian and gluten-sensitive choices, where available.

articles.title_orig: Tories pledge to halt screen-based school exams and cut coursework
articles.title_zh: Tories pledge to halt screen-based school exams and cut coursework
articles.content_orig:
The Conservatives have promised to halt screen-based exams and cut coursework in a bid to limit the use of AI by schoolchildren in England if the party returns to power.
The party has also pledged to develop new guidelines so that laptops and tablets are not the "default in classrooms".
Shadow education secretary Laura Trott cited recent warnings from clinicians that  excessive screen time could be damaging children's health, adding that "everything in schools must be safe for children and improve standards".
The government is currently developing new screen-time guidance for children and has previously said it would consult on the safety of AI in schools.
The vast majority of school exams in the UK are pen and paper based. Under the previous government led by Sir Keir Starmer, exam regulator Ofqual launched a consultation last year on the introduction of on-screen exams.
But it emphasised that pen and paper would "remain central" and that the most widely taken subjects would not be moving to digital assessments for the "foreseeable future".
In their announcement on Sunday, the Tories said they would "put a stop" to the introduction of screen-based exams, and require screen time for secondary pupils to be limited to no more than two hours a day.
The party said it would also minimise the amount of coursework in school assessments to avoid lowering educational standards "by allowing children to become overly reliant on the use of generative AI platforms".
Under the plans, primary schools would be required to keep screen use to a minimum and only use screens where necessary, such as in computing lessons.
The announcement comes after a group of more than 150 clinicians warned last month that the amount of time children in England spend on screens at school could be harming their "physical and developmental health" .
An open letter to Education Secretary Lucy Powell and Health Secretary Yvette Cooper from the clinicians said they were prescribing glasses, hearing aids and speech therapy to children "for a problem that is unintentionally being made worse in our schools".
Trott said: "I want to slash screen use in classrooms and set a new norm where screens are no longer the default. That means no screens in early years, minimal use in primary schools except where required by the curriculum."
Figures from the most recent government survey show that in 2024, most teachers (89%) used interactive whiteboards within lessons. But the survey also found that most teachers - 79% in primary and 69% in secondary - said pupils were using individual devices in fewer than a quater of lessons, or not at all.
The Tories said their plans draw on the work of the Health Professionals for Safer Screens campaign group, which has warned about the effects of excessive screen time on children.
Its founder Dr Rebecca Foljambe said: "We have become excessively preoccupied with why children are on screens. Although content is important, this distracts from the fact that daily screen time can profoundly affect a child's health, whatever they are watching or doing."
As part of its proposal, the Tories said £900m that "the government currently spends on EdTech" would be repurposed to create a £250m fund for new textbooks.
A Department for Education spokesperson said schools decided how much to spend on educational technology, which alongside screens also included things such as management information systems, from within their own budgets.
"It is up to schools to decide how they use their funding in the best interests of pupils," they said.
They added: "Building on the guidance we have published for children under 5, in the new year the department will publish clear guidance on screen use for all children aged 5 to 18, giving parents the advice they need."
A ban on smartphones in schools in England came into force in June, making individual schools and trusts legally responsible for being phone-free throughout the day.
Education is a devolved matter in the UK, with each of the four nations managing their own systems.
The UK social media ban for under-16s - banning children from major platforms such as  TikTok and Instagram - will come into force in March.

articles.title_orig: Prince Harry praises war veterans on surprise visit to Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Prince Harry praises war veterans on surprise visit to Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
The Duke of Sussex has received an enthusiastic welcome in a surprise visit to Ukraine to support injured war veterans, meeting Ukrainian competitors taking part in his Invictus Games.
There were emotional scenes as he was applauded by injured service men and women in Lviv, where he told his audience: "You're going to win the war."
Prince Harry spent two days at events for veterans, with a press blackout for security reasons until he had left Ukraine, as the country continues to face missile attacks from Russia.
Ukraine has more than 150,000 injured war veterans and the prince visited projects supporting their treatment and rehabilitation.
"Ukraine now is experiencing elements of war that no other country has experienced before," he said - with technology advancing in areas such as drone warfare, but also in protecting cities and providing treatment.
A mobile phone app is where Ukrainians look for air raid warnings, telling them the direction, timing and type of any incoming missiles.
At the Superhumans Center near Lviv, Harry was shown how growing numbers of injured veterans receive groundbreaking treatment.
International experts used to come to help Ukraine, he said, but "now that has flipped," with Ukraine having the greater expertise with trauma injuries to share with others.
That included an innovation for Mykhailo Damaskin, a Ukrainian air assault forces veteran, who was so seriously injured in fighting in Kherson he was never expected to walk again.
In an experimental treatment he had a spinal cord stimulator implanted in his back, which allows him to walk, but has to be re-charged every 12 hours. He cannot feel his feet and controls his steps using his eyes.
He needs to be plugged in and charged up to be able to move - and jokes that he is "like a demo model of a Tesla".
"My goal is to go to the Invictus Games. I promised my father before he was killed that I'd be part of the team to represent Ukraine internationally.
"I'll prove to every guy with spinal cord injuries that life goes on after injury," said Mykhailo.
At the Superhumans Center Prince Harry sat at the bedside of Konstiantyn Vlasenko, who was airlifted from the front line by a drone last month in a rescue that was a first of its kind.
He had been alone for more than 200 days and had stayed at his position, despite losing both his feet.
In a moving encounter, Prince Harry told him he represented the spirit of resilience of Ukraine.
And he described the injured veterans as "role models", promising his audience: "The rest of the world will continue to support you."
Along with all the determination, it was an inescapably poignant sight too, with so many families and children at the medical facility visiting the growing numbers of badly injured war casualties.
At a noisy sports centre, Prince Harry arrived to watch a wheelchair rugby match taking place, with some thunderous collisions between the players.
He was welcomed by the competitors in what he has called his Invictus "family" and soon the visit turned into something approaching a group hug, with Harry disappearing into a sea of selfies and handshakes.
He was presented with a T-shirt remembering prisoners of war held by Russian forces.
And he later had a chance to play one of the events at the Invictus Games, a tennis-style competition called pickleball.
Watching was Ivan Voinov, who has lost a leg and suffered head injuries, but who is using sport to help his rehabilitation - including learning to dance again.
He said that dancing was his way to be together with his wife again, which meant so much to his recovery and recovering his identity.
At an Invictus awards ceremony during the visit, Prince Harry was greeted with choruses of "Harry, Harry, Harry", getting a rock star welcome.
"Every single time I come back to Ukraine, I feel welcome, I feel warmth, I feel encouragement," he said, having returned for a fourth trip here during wartime.
He promised that "when the war is over and when Ukraine wins, we will be ready to support you in holding an Invictus Games".
There have been 400 wounded service men and women in Ukraine taking part in trials for next year's games, being hosted in Birmingham.
The sports events are an attempt to encourage rehabilitation and to recognise the resilience of people overcoming their challenges.
Prince Harry told a gathering of new Invictus members of a "cultural shift" from people being socially awkward about seeing injured veterans to wanting to show respect.
"These people have so much to offer," he said.
"Recovery cannot wait for the war to end, The scale of need in Ukraine is huge, and wounded, injured and sick service personnel and veterans need the chance to rebuild their lives now," said Rob Owen, chief executive officer of the Invictus Games Foundation.

Britain's nukes are 'not up for negotiation', Wes Streeting declared to Russia on Sunday as he marked the homecoming of a record-breaking nuclear-armed submarine.
Speaking to the Daily Mail as a tired-looking HMS Vengeance sailed into the Clyde on Sunday, the Defence Secretary insisted he would 'not abandon' European allies and cave in to 'delusional' demands by Vladimir Putin .
His comments came after it emerged Kremlin negotiators said Russia would only end its war in Ukraine if Britain agreed to stop protecting Europe with its ultimate weapons.
But Mr Streeting rejected Moscow 's proposed ceasefire ultimatum, insisting the UK's commitment to defending its allies with nuclear force was 'unwavering' and 'unshakeable'.
'The fact that Putin has made these demands demonstrates what the nuclear deterrent is, and the deterrence effect it is having in the Kremlin,' he said.
'At a dangerous time for our continent, our nuclear deterrent is not up for negotiation, and we will not abandon our allies in Nato .'
HMS Vengeance finally returned home after a record-breaking 217 days under the waves.
No other submarine has completed more than seven months under the water continuously, with Vengeance's 140-strong crew almost entirely cut off from home for it.

But challenges with maintenance have increased the demands on individual boats and their crews, meaning their patrols have increased from about three months to seven.
And the strain on Vengeance was clear to see, with barnacles, rust and algae coating the boat's stealth plating as she crept back towards her base in Faslane.
For the ship's company, the homecoming was finally a chance to return home after 'one of the most stressful jobs' the Navy can offer.
One senior submariner said the strain crews faced was immense. 'Anyone who says this would be easy is lying, it is hard,' they said. 'But we're proud to do it.'
When they set off in April, Sir Keir Starmer was still Prime Minister and the World Cup in America was still months away.
She had been due home last week, but her relief boat needed to return home for spare parts.

A pill-shaped cutout at the top-right might be an unusually placed USB-C port. The power button is on the left edge, which also has another USB-C connector at the bottom.
The removable back-cover stand appears to attach magnetically and has a diagonal fold with prominent Lenovo branding. The Glowbar sits beside the rear camera.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia is gearing up for one of Wall Street’s most anticipated earnings calls in years
articles.title_zh: Nvidia is gearing up for one of Wall Street’s most anticipated earnings calls in years
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Time was that earnings reports from chip giant Nvidia provided moments of celebration for the extraordinary success of a U.S. original who led it for 33 years.
Nvidia NVDA became the world's most valuable company (until recently) because its graphical processing chips made artificial intelligence possible and has set off the massive wave of data center development around the world.
The results for the company's third fiscal quarter, to be reported after the market close on Nov. 17, will be terrific, at least on the surface. Nvidia's revenue should be around $109 billion, up nearly 50% from a year ago and up about 13% from the second quarter, according to Opening Bell Daily .
Earnings per share are expected to hit $2.48, up from $1.30 a year ago and 11.7% from the second quarter.
Read More: Jensen Huang was 'broken and shattered' in final hours as Nvidia CEO
Would that the earnings and the analyst call that follows were so simple.
Nvidia and its investors have been going through a major soul-wrenching since Oct. 29, when The New York Times reported on CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang's involvement with Alice Huang, a woman whom intelligence officials believe was a Chinese spy. Then, reports broke that Jensen Huang had had affairs with two company employees.
Nvidia shares rose nearly 4,000% between the end of 2019 and its closing peak of $239.24 on Oct. 6, making Jensen Huang a rock star among corporate bosses — and a confidante of President Donald Trump.
But it all ended with his resignation on Nov. 12.
Nvidia's shares are off 24% since the Oct. 29 story broke. Worse, they're off 33% since reaching a 52-week high of $243.37 on Oct. 6. When the shares closed that day (at $239.24), they were up 28.3% for the year.
And as of Nov. 13 (when the stock fell 2% to $162.85), Nvidia is down 12.7% for the year.
No fewer than nine investment houses downgraded their opinions on the stock. Two cut their price targets.
Nvidia's 60% target cut exposes a Wall Street split
Nvidia has a stake in SpaceX that came from an unexpected place
Nvidia's $12.9 billion deal could shape the AI apps you use
Nvidia will demand attention and not just because Jensen Huang is no longer CEO. The earnings call will be run by interim CEO Colette Kress, who has been Nvidia's executive vice president and chief financial officer since 2013.
In addition to questions to interim CEO Kress about the company's outlook, analysts may well probe:
The China spying scandal. Jensen Huang's involvement with Alice Huang is an issue because she was an executive at Megaspeed, a company in Singapore that bought Nvidia chips and related equipment and software ostensibly for distribution in South America.
But the allegations are that Megaspeed diverted the products to Chinese companies in violation of U.S. export rules. (For several years, reports have suggested that companies in Singapore would buy Nvidia equipment, repackage it and ship it to China.)
Nvidia's bankrolling activities . At the end of the second quarter, Nvidia owned $47 billion in stock and other securities in publicly traded companies, according to its second-quarter Securities & Exchange Commission filing . As important: It also owned $48 billion in securities in non-public companies, the filing says.
It is believed $30 billion of that total is in OpenAI, which remains a private company. It has committed to investing $10 billion in Anthropic after its IPO. In addition, the company has been helping smaller customers buy Nvidia chips by offering credit terms.
Nvidia's succession planning. When Jensen Huang resigned, Nvidia had no succession plan. Moreover, Huang is 63. So it is now looking for a new CEO, a process that may take a year or more. (President Trump has nominated former Apple CEO Tim Cook for the job, although he is still Apple's executive chairman.)
Nvidia's organization chart. Huang also ran Nvidia with a very horizontal organization with some 60 executives reporting directly to him. An Inc. magazine article derided the structure. "Designing a company where every road runs through the founder's desk does not just cut red tape. It plants a live grenade under your company's valuation."
The bulk of Nvidia's business is with the so-called hyperscalers, including Google-parent Alphabet ( GOOGL ), Amazon.com ( AMZN ), Microsoft ( MSFT ) and Meta Platforms ( META ). It also owns stakes in companies such as CoreWeave ( CRWV ) and Nebius ( NBIS ).
By the end of the week, most of the media talk about the stock market ahead was basically about Nvidia, which doesn't do justice for what will be a week of important earnings and economic reports.
And, oh yes, the projected initial public offering of Anthropic, due after the Nov. 18 close with trading expected to begin on Nov. 19.
Earnings scheduled for release next week include Walt Disney ( DIS ), Home Depot ( HD ), Lowe's Companies ( LOW ), Target ( TGT ) and Walmart ( WMT ).
Plus there will be lots of talk about Friday's grounding of all commercial aircraft. The grounding may affect airline stocks.
For all the attention lavished on Nvidia, stocks had a fairly good week, with the Standard & Poor's 500 Index up 2.5% to 7,562. The Nasdaq Composite Index added 2.5% on the week, despite a loss on Nov. 13. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 2.1% on the week to 52,348.
A number of the biggest retailers will be reporting next week, ending on Thursday with Walmart.
The key question for all of them, especially Home Depot and Lowe's Companies, will be to describe consumer health and confidence.
Business for Home Depot, due before the Nov. 17 open, and Lowe's, due a day later, depends a great deal on whether people are buying homes or renovating their homes, and interest rates have been a challenge.
Two economic reports will reinforce that question:
The Housing Market Index from the National Association of Home Builders, due Nov. 17 at 10 a.m. ET.
The Commerce Department's report on October housing starts, due on Nov. 18.

Having fans design their own Robot Masters has always been one of the more interesting parts of the series, and Cleanser Man certainly fits right in. Now I’m curious to see how his boss fight plays out and, more importantly, what weapon Mega Man gets after putting him in his place.
